How source maps leak in production

A source map only becomes a problem when a production deployment leaves it publicly reachable. There are four common, independent ways that happens, and each has its own fix -- fixing one does not fix the others.

1. The dev devtool setting shipped to production

Many starter configs use the same devtool (webpack) or build.sourcemap (Vite) setting for both dev and prod builds. webpack's plain 'source-map' mode writes a full map with sourcesContent and adds a //# sourceMappingURL= comment to the shipped script -- exactly what you want on your own machine, and exactly what you don't want served publicly. 

// webpack.config.js
module.exports = {
  devtool: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'
    ? 'hidden-source-map'   // map is still generated, but no comment references it
    : 'eval-source-map',    // fast, full detail, dev only
};

hidden-source-map still produces a real map you can upload to an error-tracking service (Sentry and similar all support this) for real stack traces on production errors -- it just never adds the reference a browser (or this checker) would follow.

2. The deploy step copies .map files it shouldn't

Even with the right devtool mode, a build step that copies the whole output directory to the CDN or server will ship any .map file still sitting on disk. Exclude it explicitly: 

# rsync example
rsync -av --exclude='*.map' dist/ user@host:/var/www/app/

3. No server/CDN rule blocking .map as a second layer

Defense in depth: even if a map ends up in the deploy artifact by accident, a rule that returns 404 for any path ending in .map means the script's own reference leads nowhere. This is the "blocked" result this checker reports as the healthy outcome when a reference exists but the file itself is not actually served. 

# nginx example
location ~ \.map$ {
  return 404;
}

4. A vendor or third-party bundle carries its own reference

A pre-built vendor chunk -- a bundled UI library, an analytics SDK, anything pulled in as a finished artifact rather than compiled from your own source -- can carry its own sourceMappingURL comment independently of your build config. Check every script tag the page actually loads, not just the entry bundle you wrote yourself.

Run the Source Map Leak Checker against your production URL (or paste the specific script URLs) to see which of these, if any, apply to your deployment right now. Only run it against a site you own or are authorised to test.

ScriptResultDetail

Prefer a CLI, or hit a CORS wall in the browser?

Most sites don't send permissive CORS headers on their main HTML document, so a browser tab often cannot read a cross-origin page's HTML at all — you'll see a generic network error with no HTTP status. Static JS/CSS assets on many CDNs and static hosts are more often served with permissive CORS, so pasting explicit script URLs above has better odds than a bare page URL. The CLI has no such restriction and is the one path guaranteed to complete: 

node check.mjs https://example.com/ --json
node check.mjs --script https://example.com/static/main.js --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if any script's map is exposed, so you can gate a deploy on it.

Common questions

What is a source map, and why would it be a problem?

A source map is a file (usually named <script>.js.map) that maps a minified, bundled production script back to its original, unminified source files -- so a browser's devtools can show you readable code and real file names while debugging a live site. Most bundlers (webpack, esbuild, Vite, Rollup) can generate one automatically. The problem is that a source map with sourcesContent set doesn't just map locations back to file names -- it embeds the entire original, unminified source text of every file, including comments, internal variable and function names, and anything that was only removed by minification rather than deliberately kept out of the client bundle.

Isn't this exactly what source maps are for -- readable code in devtools?

Yes, for a developer working on their own local build. The exposure is specifically about a production deployment: if the .map file is left publicly reachable on the live site, anyone who opens devtools (or just requests the .map URL directly, whether or not they open devtools) can read it -- not just the site's own developers. Bundler docs generally recommend either omitting the sourceMappingURL comment in production, restricting access to the map file at the server/CDN level, or using a 'hidden' source map mode that uploads the map to an error-tracking service (for real stack traces) without ever referencing it from the shipped script. See how source maps leak in production for the common ways this happens and how to fix each one.

What can someone actually learn from an exposed map?

It depends on whether the map carries sourcesContent. Without it, an exposed map still reveals the original file and folder structure of the app -- useful reconnaissance about what framework and internal module layout is in use. With sourcesContent present, it hands over the complete original source: internal comments, business logic, API endpoint paths that were only referenced by variable name in the minified bundle, and occasionally a hardcoded value (a test key, an internal URL) a developer never meant to ship in readable form.

Is it safe to point this at a URL?

This tool sends only ordinary GET requests to the page and script/map URLs you name -- the same requests your own browser already makes when you load the page, and it never writes or submits anything. It does not upload the URL, the scripts, or anything they contain to our servers when run in the browser; every request goes straight from your browser to the target. Still, only run this against a site you own or are authorised to test, the same caution you would apply to any request tool aimed at someone else's server.

Does a clean report mean my site is safe?

It means the scripts this run could check either had no source map reference or had one that was not publicly readable at the time of the check. It does not check CSS source maps, inline (non-external) scripts, JS loaded by dynamic import after the initial page load, or anything not reachable from the page or script list you gave it. Treat a clean report as evidence about the scripts this run actually saw, not a full audit of the site. See how this compares to checking devtools by hand.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks only the scripts a run could reach from the page or list you gave it, using one GET request per script and (when referenced) one per map. It never writes, submits, or modifies anything, does not check CSS source maps, inline scripts, or dynamically-imported JS, and cannot see an exposure it never fetched. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the site has no exposure.

Source Map Leak Checker vs. checking devtools by hand

Opening a browser's devtools and looking at the Sources/Debugger panel is a real, fast way to spot the single obvious case: a map that is fully exposed on the exact script you happened to open. It is also the method most developers already reach for first, and it genuinely works for that case. This page is not affiliated with any browser vendor — it names browser devtools only as a generic manual habit, not a product being compared against.

CheckOpening devtools by handThis tool
Obvious fully-exposed map on the script you're looking atCatches itCatches it
A map reference that 404s/403s (stray but harmless)Easy to misread as "no map"Reports it separately as "blocked", distinct from "clean"
A vendor/third-party bundle with its own referenceEasy to skip — you're looking at your own entry bundleChecks every script tag the page loads
An inline data: URI source mapEasy to miss scanning network requestsDecoded and checked the same as an external map
Repeatable in CI on every deployManual, point-in-timeCLI returns a real exit code
Distinguishes full source text from paths-onlyYou'd have to read the map JSON yourselfReported automatically as a separate severity

When to still just look

If you only need a one-off sanity check on a page you're already staring at in devtools, looking is fine — it's free and you're already there. The gap this tool closes is coverage: every script tag, not just the one you opened, checked the same way every time a deploy happens, with an exit code a CI pipeline can act on.

Common questions

What does opening devtools by hand actually show you?

Open the Sources (Chrome/Edge) or Debugger (Firefox) panel on a live page: if a script's map is loaded, you'll usually see the original, readable file tree instead of the minified bundle. That is a fast, real signal for the single obvious case -- a map that is fully exposed on the exact script you happened to open.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Three ways this scripted check catches and a quick devtools look easily misses: (1) a script that references a map which 404s or 403s -- devtools just shows you the minified code with no indication of whether the reference itself is a stray leftover or was never a problem; you'd have to separately try to load the .map URL. (2) A vendor or third-party bundle carrying its own sourceMappingURL comment independently of your own build -- easy to skip when you're eyeballing the entry bundle you wrote and not the ten other script tags the page also loads. (3) An inline data: URI source map, which some bundlers embed directly in the script rather than as a separate file -- devtools will resolve it the same way, but a person scanning file sizes or thinking 'no separate .map request, so no map' would miss it.

Why does this matter for CI, not just a one-time check?

A devtools check is a point-in-time, manual look. A deploy pipeline, a CDN config change, or a new vendor dependency can reintroduce an exposed map at any point after the last time someone happened to look. The CLI here returns a real exit code, so it can gate a deploy the same way a linter or test suite does -- catching a regression the day it ships rather than the next time someone thinks to check by hand.
